title: Dry-run: a trie with precomputed top-k

spec.title: Dry-run: a trie with precomputed top-k
spec.intro: About 5 minutes. Build the plain trie first, show it collapsing on a hot prefix, then precompute. The collapse is the whole reason the real design exists.

steps.title: The plain trie
steps.explain: Start with the obvious structure — a tree of characters where each terminal node holds a frequency. Walking to a prefix is a handful of pointer hops, essentially free.
steps.saysOutLoud: Finding the prefix node is O(p) and cheap. The problem is what comes after.

steps.title: Break it on a one-letter prefix
steps.explain: To rank completions you must visit every descendant and sort. For 'zyg' that is a few nodes; for 'a' it is a large fraction of the entire trie — on a request that must finish under 100 ms. And 'a' is far more common than 'zyg', so the slowest case is also the most frequent one.
steps.saysOutLoud: The worst case here is also the most popular query — that's why this doesn't ship.

steps.title: Store the answer at every node
steps.explain: Trade space and build time for a flat read. Once each node carries its own top-k, lookup is a walk plus an array read — and it no longer matters whether the prefix is 'a' or 'zyg', because the work is identical either way.

steps.title: Build top-k bottom-up, in one pass
steps.explain: A node's top-k is derivable from its children's, so a single post-order pass computes the whole structure. Re-scanning descendants per node would be quadratic — this is the detail that makes the build tractable.
steps.saysOutLoud: One post-order pass — each node merges its children's lists rather than rescanning.

steps.title: Bound the storage cost
steps.explain: Every node now carries k entries, which multiplies memory. Two mitigations keep it sane, and both are worth naming because they show you have thought about the cost rather than only the speed.

steps.title: The trie is immutable and swapped, never mutated
steps.explain: A batch pipeline builds a fresh trie offline and the serving tier flips a pointer to it, letting in-flight requests finish against the old one. This removes concurrent mutation from the only component with a hard latency budget — and it is bought entirely by accepting that suggestions may be minutes stale.

steps.title: Filter at serving time, not build time
steps.explain: Fetch k plus a margin and drop blocked terms before returning. Filtering here rather than at build time means a newly-discovered problem term disappears in seconds instead of at the next rebuild — and suggestions are put in users' mouths, so that latency matters.
steps.saysOutLoud: I filter on read so a blocklist update takes effect immediately.

steps.title: Check whether you even need to shard
steps.explain: Say this before reaching for sharding. With capped depth and ID-based lists the trie plausibly fits in memory on one machine, so you replicate instead — strictly simpler. Sharding a trie is awkward and hot-spots on common letters.

spec.closing: If they ask about load: debouncing ~50 ms on the client turns 8 keystrokes into 2–3 requests. The cheapest request is the one never sent, and it costs nothing to mention.
